title: Fallout shelter basics: where to shelter from radioactive fallout, and what shields you
asks: where is the best place to shelter from fallout
what makes a good fallout shelter
is my basement a good fallout shelter
is a car safe from fallout

how much dirt or concrete stops fallout radiation

answer: The best protection from fallout radiation is underground (basements, subway tunnels, underground parking garages) or in the center of a large, heavy building.
Inside, stay away from windows, corners, doors, outside walls and the roof.
An adequate shelter reduces the radiation dose by a factor of 10 or more. Examples: basements; the centers of large, multi-story structures; parking garages; tunnels.
Cars and other vehicles are not adequate shelters: they lack dense shielding material. Single-story wood-frame houses without basements also provide only limited shielding.

Any shelter is better than being outside for extended periods of time. A smaller wood or steel frame house does not usually provide adequate protection above ground, but it is still far better than being outside. Thicker-walled masonry buildings and residential basements generally provide adequate protection.

Good shielding materials are concrete, brick, stone and earth. Wood, drywall and thin sheet metal provide minimal shielding, but many layers of them can also provide adequate protection, for example a central room with many walls in between.
To protect against fallout radiation: reduce the time spent in radioactive areas, increase your distance from the fallout, and use dense materials (concrete, brick or earth) as shielding.
A shelter does not need to be airtight. A building with minor damage can be used if it is structurally sound, and even buildings with broken windows can provide adequate protection.
Close windows and doors to minimize the outdoor air drawn into the building, but maintain enough ventilation for adequate indoor air quality.

A 3-foot thickness of earth, or a 2-foot thickness of concrete, is an effective barrier: it absorbs about 99.9% of the gamma rays from fallout. About 3.6 inches (9 centimeters) of packed earth reduces by half the radiation dose that passes through it.
For good protection you must be shielded overhead and on all sides.
It is best to be in the shelter when the fallout arrives.

How long: FEMA says to plan to remain sheltered for at least 12 to 24 hours. The Oak Ridge nuclear war survival manual says that within two weeks after an attack the occupants of most shelters could safely stop using them, or could work outside for an increasing number of hours each day, except in areas of extremely heavy fallout.
To know when it is safe to come out, you need a reliable fallout meter, or information based on measurements made nearby with a reliable instrument.
warnings: In the first few hours, lethal radiation levels may be present even tens of miles from ground zero and where fallout is not apparent. The hazard decreases significantly over time.
Immediate threats to life take priority: leaving the shelter may be warranted in the event of fire, building collapse or a medical emergency.

The best initial action following a nuclear explosion is moving to and remaining within an accessible, adequate shelter away from windows, corners, doors, and outside walls. Individuals should plan to remain sheltered for at least 12‒24 hours.
Stay away from the outer walls and roof. This will help provide protection from the blast, heat, and radiation of the detonation.

Adequate shelters reduce radiation doses by a factor of 10 or more and examples include basements; centers of large, multi-story structures; parking garages, and tunnels. Cars and other vehicles are not adequate shelters because they lack dense shielding material. Good shielding materials include concrete, brick, stone, and earth. Wood, drywall, and thin sheet metal provide minimal shielding. However, many layers of minimal shielding materials can also provide adequate protection (e.g., central rooms with many intervening drywalls). Structures do not need to be airtight to protect against fallout radiation, so buildings with minor damage can be used as shelters if they are structurally sound.
Vehicles and single-story wood frame houses without basements provide limited shielding and should not be considered adequate shelter.
It is best to be in a shelter when fallout arrives. Any shelter is better than being outside for extended periods of time.

Smaller single-family homes, particularly wood/steel frame houses, do not usually provide adequate protection above ground, though is still far better than being outside. Thickerwalled masonry buildings and residential basements generally provide adequate protection.

Fallout exposure can be effectively minimized by taking shelter in a protective structure. The outdoor radiation hazard from fallout (often referred to as the “ground shine dose”) is typically orders of magnitude more hazardous than internal exposure concerns resulting from inhalation or ingestion of radioactive material. Even buildings with broken windows can provide adequate protection from ground shine dose.
Close windows and doors to minimize the amount of outdoor air being drawn into the building. Make sure to maintain enough ventilation to ensure adequate indoor air quality.
The 3-foot thickness of earth shown (or a 2-foot thickness of concrete) will provide an effective barrier, attenuating (absorbing) about 99.9% of all gamma rays from fallout.
Each of the layers shown is one halving-thickness of packed earth-about 3.6 inches (9 centimeters).
A halvingthickness is the thickness of a material which reduces by half the dose of radiation that passes through it.
For good protection he must be protected overhead and on all sides by barrier shielding.

Within two weeks after an attack the occupants of most shelters could safely stop using them, or could work outside the shelters for an increasing number of hours each day. Exceptions would be in areas of extremely heavy fallout such as might occur downwind from important targets attacked with many weapons, especially missile sites and very large cities. To know when to come out safely, occupants either would need a reliable fallout meter to measure the changing radiation dangers, or must receive information based on measurements made nearby with a reliable instrument.

In the first few hours, lethal radiation levels may be present―even in areas tens of miles from ground zero and/or where fallout is not apparent. The hazard of the fallout radiation will decrease significantly over time, enabling safer evacuations.
As with all guidance, immediate threats to life take priority, so evacuation may be warranted in the event of fire, building collapse, or medical emergencies.

conflict: How long to stay sheltered: the sources describe different scenarios and give different times. FEMA (single detonation): Are You Ready (2020) 'Stay inside for 24 hours unless local authorities provide other instructions'; Planning Guidance (2022) 'at least 12-24 hours'; First 72 Hours (2023) 'at least the first 24 hours'. ORNL-5037 (1979, all-out attack): 'Within two weeks after an attack the occupants of most shelters could safely stop using them', longer in areas of extremely heavy fallout. The card shows the FEMA planning figure and the ORNL figure side by side. Also, on vehicles: FEMA (2022) says 'Cars and other vehicles are not adequate shelters because they lack dense shielding material'; HHS Ship's Medicine Chest (2003), written for responders near a radiation source, says 'If possible, use clothing, vehicles, equipment, containers or natural barriers like hills, trees, and rocks to protect yourself from radiation exposure', adding that they 'may not provide adequate shielding'. The card gives only FEMA's fallout-shelter statement.
